lessonTitle: Mechanics of Breathing and Lung Volumes

blocks.text: A baby born at 28 weeks of gestation is breathing fast, grunting and drawing in the skin between the ribs with each breath, and a chest X-ray shows a fine ground-glass appearance. Her lungs are stiff and tend to collapse at the end of every breath because her alveoli do not yet make enough surfactant. To understand why, we must look at how the lungs are inflated, how volumes are measured, and what forces keep air sacs open.

blocks.markdown: Air moves in and out of the lungs because pressure differences are created by the respiratory muscles. During quiet inspiration the **diaphragm** contracts and flattens (with help from the external intercostal muscles), enlarging the thorax. Intrapleural pressure, normally slightly below atmospheric pressure, becomes more negative, the lungs expand, alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive, driven by the elastic recoil of the lungs. At rest the inward recoil of the lungs is balanced by the outward spring of the chest wall; the lung volume at which these forces balance is the **functional residual capacity (FRC)**.

blocks.caption: Lung compliance: the volume change (L) produced by a unit change in distending pressure (cmH2O). A normal value is around 0.2 L/cmH2O. Low compliance means a stiff lung.

rows: Volume inspired or expired in one quiet breath
Extra volume that can be inspired after a quiet inspiration
Extra volume that can be expired after a quiet expiration
Volume remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration
ERV + RV: volume in the lungs at the end of quiet expiration
IRV + TV + ERV: maximum volume that can be expired after a maximal inspiration
VC + RV: volume in the lungs after maximal inspiration
blocks.caption: Lung volumes and capacities for a typical young adult man. Values depend on sex, height, age and ethnicity. A capacity is the sum of two or more volumes.

blocks.title: Identifying volumes from a spirometry trace
blocks.prompt: A spirometer trace of a healthy adult shows quiet tidal breathing with a tidal volume of 0.5 L, a maximal inspiration adding 3.0 L above end-tidal inspiration, and a maximal expiration removing 1.1 L below end-tidal expiration. The residual volume is measured separately by helium dilution as 1.2 L. Calculate VC, FRC and TLC.

steps.text: Vital capacity is the maximal volume exhaled after maximal inspiration: IRV + TV + ERV.
Functional residual capacity is what remains after a quiet expiration: ERV + RV.
Total lung capacity is VC + RV.

blocks.answer: VC is 4.6 L, FRC is 2.3 L and TLC is 5.8 L.

blocks.title: What spirometry cannot measure
blocks.text: A spirometer records only air that moves in and out of the mouth. It therefore cannot measure residual volume, and so cannot measure FRC or TLC, which both include RV. These require gas dilution (for example with helium) or body plethysmography. On a trace, TV, IRV, ERV, IC and VC can be identified directly as vertical distances.

blocks.markdown: **Surfactant.** The inside of every alveolus is lined with a thin film of fluid, and the air-liquid interface has **surface tension**, the cohesive force between water molecules that tends to shrink the surface. This tension is a major part of the lung's elastic recoil. **Pulmonary surfactant** is a mixture of phospholipids (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and proteins secreted by **type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes)**. Its molecules sit at the air-liquid interface, interrupting the cohesion between water molecules and reducing surface tension.

blocks.caption: Laplace's law for a single liquid-lined sphere: P is the pressure needed to keep it inflated (Pa), T the surface tension (N/m) and r the radius (m).

blocks.title: Laplace's law and alveolar stability
blocks.prompt: An alveolus of radius 100 micrometres (1.0 x 10^-4 m) has a surface tension of 0.050 N/m without surfactant, and 0.010 N/m with surfactant. Calculate the distending pressure in each case, and state what happens to the pressure if the radius halves while the tension stays the same.

steps.text: If the radius halves while T stays the same, P doubles, so a smaller alveolus would develop a higher pressure and tend to empty into a larger neighbour.

blocks.answer: Surfactant lowers the distending pressure five-fold (from about 10 to about 2 cmH2O). Without it, small alveoli would have a higher pressure and would collapse into larger ones.

blocks.title: Functions of surfactant
blocks.text: Surfactant (1) reduces surface tension, which increases lung compliance and reduces the work of breathing; (2) stabilises alveoli of different sizes, because its concentration rises as an alveolus shrinks, lowering tension more in small alveoli and preventing them collapsing into larger ones (atelectasis); and (3) reduces the tendency to draw fluid from capillaries into the alveoli, helping keep them dry. Deficiency in premature infants causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

blocks.markdown: **Obstructive and restrictive patterns.** In a forced expiratory manoeuvre the subject breathes in fully and then exhales as hard and fast as possible. The total volume expelled is the **forced vital capacity (FVC)**, and the volume expelled in the first second is the **forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)**. The ratio FEV1/FVC is normally about 0.75 to 0.85 in healthy young adults; a value below about 0.7 is commonly taken as airflow obstruction, though cut-offs vary between guidelines and with age. In **obstructive disease** (for example asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) airway narrowing slows emptying, so FEV1 falls much more than FVC and the ratio falls. In **restrictive disease** (for example pulmonary fibrosis or chest wall or neuromuscular disorders) the lungs cannot expand fully, so FVC and FEV1 fall proportionately and the ratio is normal or high.

rows: Normal or mildly reduced (air trapping may reduce it)
Increased airway resistance or loss of elastic recoil
Reduced compliance of lung or chest wall, or weak muscles
blocks.caption: Distinguishing obstructive from restrictive patterns on spirometry. Obstruction is confirmed by the ratio; a reduced FVC with a normal ratio suggests restriction, which needs lung volume measurement to confirm.

blocks.title: Classifying two patients
blocks.prompt: Patient A has FEV1 1.8 L and FVC 3.6 L. Patient B has FEV1 2.4 L and FVC 2.8 L; her FVC is 60 per cent of the predicted value for her age and size. Calculate FEV1/FVC for each and classify the pattern.

steps.text: This is well below 0.7, so patient A has an obstructive pattern: the lungs hold a reasonable volume but empty slowly.
The ratio is normal or high, but FVC is low at 60 per cent of predicted, a restrictive pattern: the lungs are small and stiff, but emptying is not slowed.

blocks.answer: Patient A: ratio 0.50, obstructive. Patient B: ratio 0.86 with low FVC, restrictive.

blocks.title: A low FVC alone does not prove restriction
blocks.text: In severe obstruction air trapping can also reduce FVC, so a low FVC with a low ratio is still obstructive. True restriction is a reduced total lung capacity, which spirometry alone cannot prove because it cannot measure TLC.

points: Inspiration is active (diaphragm, external intercostals); quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil; FRC is the volume at which lung recoil and chest wall spring balance.
Spirometry measures TV, IRV, ERV, IC and VC directly but not RV, FRC or TLC, which need gas dilution or plethysmography.

Surfactant, made by type II pneumocytes, lowers surface tension, increases compliance, and stabilises alveoli of different sizes in accordance with Laplace's law (P = 2T/r); deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
Obstructive disease reduces FEV1 more than FVC, so FEV1/FVC falls (below about 0.7); restrictive disease reduces FEV1 and FVC proportionately so the ratio is normal or high.

questions.stem: Which expression correctly defines vital capacity?

options.text: Tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume
Inspiratory reserve volume plus tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume
Expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume
Vital capacity plus residual volume

questions.correctOptionText: Inspiratory reserve volume plus tidal volume plus expiratory reserve volume

distractorRationale.a: This omits the inspiratory reserve volume.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: VC = IRV + TV + ERV, the maximal volume expired after maximal inspiration.
distractorRationale.c: This is the functional residual capacity.
distractorRationale.d: This is the total lung capacity.

questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the largest volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration, and equals IRV + TV + ERV. Adding the residual volume gives the total lung capacity.

questions.stem: A small adult woman has a tidal volume of 0.45 L, an inspiratory reserve volume of 2.40 L, an expiratory reserve volume of 0.90 L and a residual volume of 1.00 L. Calculate her total lung capacity in litres.
questions.explanation: Vital capacity is IRV + TV + ERV = 2.40 + 0.45 + 0.90 = 3.75 L. Adding the residual volume of 1.00 L gives a total lung capacity of 4.75 L.

questions.stem: Which of the following cannot be measured by simple spirometry?

options.text: Tidal volume
Vital capacity
Functional residual capacity
Expiratory reserve volume

distractorRationale.a: Tidal volume is recorded directly as the excursion of quiet breathing.
distractorRationale.b: Vital capacity is recorded directly from maximal inspiration to maximal expiration.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: FRC includes the residual volume, which cannot be expired and so cannot be measured by a spirometer.
distractorRationale.d: Expiratory reserve volume is the maximal expiration after a quiet breath and is recorded directly.

questions.explanation: A spirometer records only air that moves in and out of the mouth. Functional residual capacity includes the residual volume that always stays in the lungs, so it needs gas dilution or body plethysmography.

questions.stem: Alveoli of different sizes are connected to the same airways. Why does surfactant help prevent small alveoli from collapsing and emptying into larger ones?

options.text: It increases surface tension more in small alveoli, equalising pressure
It reduces surface tension to a greater degree in small alveoli, because its molecules are more concentrated there, offsetting the rise in pressure predicted by Laplace's law
It increases the radius of every alveolus equally
It stiffens the alveolar wall, making it incompressible

questions.correctOptionText: It reduces surface tension to a greater degree in small alveoli, because its molecules are more concentrated there, offsetting the rise in pressure predicted by Laplace's law

distractorRationale.a: Surfactant lowers, not raises, surface tension.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: in P = 2T/r, a smaller r raises P; surfactant lowers T most in small alveoli, preventing their collapse.
distractorRationale.c: Surfactant does not change alveolar radius directly.
distractorRationale.d: Surfactant does not stiffen the wall; it makes the lung more compliant.

questions.explanation: Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) predicts that small alveoli would have higher pressure and empty into larger ones. Surfactant molecules become more concentrated as an alveolus shrinks, reducing T by more, so pressures are more equal and alveoli are stable.

questions.stem: Which combination of effects is expected when alveolar surfactant is deficient?

options.text: Higher surface tension, lower lung compliance, increased work of breathing and a tendency to alveolar collapse
Lower surface tension, higher compliance and reduced work of breathing
Higher surface tension with higher compliance and alveolar over-distension
No change in surface tension but airway narrowing

questions.correctOptionText: Higher surface tension, lower lung compliance, increased work of breathing and a tendency to alveolar collapse

distractorRationale.a: Correct: without surfactant, surface tension rises, so the lungs are stiff and alveoli collapse.
distractorRationale.b: These are the effects of surfactant being present, not absent.
distractorRationale.c: Higher surface tension makes the lung stiffer (lower compliance), not more compliant.
distractorRationale.d: Surface tension changes directly when surfactant is deficient.

questions.explanation: Without surfactant, surface tension at the air-liquid interface is high. This makes the lung stiff (low compliance), raises the work of breathing and favours atelectasis, as in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: A model alveolus is a sphere of radius 150 micrometres (1.5 x 10^-4 m) with a surface tension of 0.030 N/m. Using Laplace's law for a single liquid-lined sphere, calculate the distending pressure in pascals.
questions.explanation: Laplace's law gives P = 2T / r = 2 x 0.030 / 1.5 x 10^-4 = 400 Pa, which is about 4 cmH2O. Halving the surface tension (as surfactant does) would halve this pressure, which helps keep the alveolus open at a low inflation pressure.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years has a forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) of 1.5 L and a forced vital capacity (FVC) of 3.5 L. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Restrictive pattern, because the FVC is low
Normal spirometry, because FEV1 and FVC are both within the usual range
Obstructive pattern, because FEV1/FVC is about 0.43
Restrictive pattern, because FEV1/FVC is above 0.8

questions.correctOptionText: Obstructive pattern, because FEV1/FVC is about 0.43

distractorRationale.a: A restrictive pattern needs a proportional fall in FEV1 and FVC with a normal or high ratio; here the ratio is low.
distractorRationale.b: The ratio is markedly reduced, so the spirometry is not normal.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: 1.5 / 3.5 = 0.43, well below 0.7, indicating airflow obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio is not above 0.8; it is about 0.43.

questions.explanation: FEV1/FVC is 1.5 / 3.5 = 0.43, well below the 0.7 threshold, so airflow is obstructed. This is typical of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, where narrowed airways slow the emptying of the lungs.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with progressive breathlessness has an FEV1 of 2.2 L and an FVC of 2.5 L, which is 55 per cent of her predicted value. Which statement fits these findings?

options.text: The ratio is about 0.88, in keeping with a restrictive pattern such as pulmonary fibrosis
The ratio is about 0.50, in keeping with an obstructive pattern
The ratio is about 0.88, in keeping with an obstructive pattern
The ratio cannot be calculated

questions.correctOptionText: The ratio is about 0.88, in keeping with a restrictive pattern such as pulmonary fibrosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 2.2 / 2.5 = 0.88, a high ratio with a reduced FVC, suggesting restriction.
distractorRationale.c: A ratio of 0.88 is not obstructive.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio is simply FEV1 divided by FVC.

questions.explanation: FEV1/FVC = 2.2 / 2.5 = 0.88 is normal or high, while FVC is markedly reduced. This combination is the signature of a restrictive process such as pulmonary fibrosis, in which the lungs are small and stiff but air flows out quickly.

questions.stem: Explain the role of pulmonary surfactant in reducing surface tension and preventing alveolar collapse. Include Laplace's law, the cells that make surfactant, and one consequence of deficiency.
markingGuide: Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells (pneumocytes) and is mainly phospholipid (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) with proteins
It sits at the air-liquid interface and reduces surface tension by interrupting cohesion between water molecules
Laplace's law: P = 2T/r, so without surfactant a small alveolus would have a higher pressure and empty into a larger one
Surfactant lowers tension more in smaller alveoli (greater concentration), so alveoli of different sizes remain stable
It increases compliance and reduces the work of breathing
Deficiency (for example in premature infants) causes stiff lungs and alveolar collapse: neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
questions.explanation: Surfactant from type II cells lowers surface tension, which by Laplace's law reduces the pressure needed to keep alveoli inflated and makes the lungs more compliant. Because its effect is greatest in small alveoli, it prevents them from collapsing into larger ones, and its absence in a premature infant leads to stiff, collapsing lungs.

questions.stem: Distinguish an obstructive from a restrictive spirometry pattern in terms of FEV1, FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio, and explain the physiological mechanism of each pattern. Give one example disease of each.
markingGuide: Defines FEV1 as the volume exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration after a full inspiration, and FVC as the total volume forcibly exhaled
Obstructive: FEV1 reduced much more than FVC, so FEV1/FVC is low (below about 0.7)
Obstructive mechanism: increased airway resistance or loss of elastic recoil slows emptying (air trapping may raise residual volume and total lung capacity)
Obstructive example: asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Restrictive: FEV1 and FVC both reduced proportionately, so the ratio is normal or high
Restrictive mechanism: reduced lung or chest wall compliance, or muscle weakness, limiting expansion (total lung capacity reduced)
Restrictive example: pulmonary fibrosis, chest wall deformity or neuromuscular disease
questions.explanation: In obstruction, airway narrowing slows expiratory flow so FEV1 falls more than FVC and the ratio drops. In restriction, the lungs or chest cannot expand fully so volumes fall proportionately and emptying is not slowed, leaving the ratio normal or high.
